source: Zhang, Kweon, Han (2026) How Strongly Should Task State Influence an LLM Agent?
finding: Controlled ladder on the same model and episodes: raw transcript, accurate checklist shown, directives, enforcement gate. A hard gate that refuses state-violating actions beats the same state shown as text.
numbers: Qwen3-235B, no thinking, amended brief, 128 episodes per cell, strict success. S=10: checklist 0.55, self-written ledger 0.70, directive gate 0.84, enforcement gate 0.98. S=15 dense: 0.59, 0.79, 0.87, 0.98. Raw transcript 0.38 (S=10), 0.50 (S=15). Qwen3.6-35B: gate 0.97 vs directive 0.75.
quote: Enforcement helps when failures are state-decidable and frequent, and hurts when the gate's judgement is wrong
limits: One synthetic booking-style task family with compiled state; gate needs correct state and a correct matcher. Tool-harness results use only 50 episodes per arm. Preprint, not peer reviewed. Read through a fetch tool summary of the HTML, not line by line.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to gap 1. For must-not-skip items that a program can decide, enforcement code beats advice in the prompt by a wide margin. Guardrails that need judgement should not be hard-gated.

source: Zhang, Kweon, Han (2026) How Strongly Should Task State Influence an LLM Agent? (boundary cases)
finding: Gate benefit depends on how often the agent violates the rule and on gate accuracy. Where the agent rarely errs, or the matcher is poor, the gate gives nothing or hurts. With thinking switched on, the ladder compresses.
numbers: tau2-bench airline: Qwen3-235B pass^1 0.39 (transcript) to 0.54 (gate); Qwen3.6-35B unchanged (rarely violates policy). PM-Bench: showing the record was best; Qwen3.6-35B transcript 0.63, checklist 0.72, directives 0.72, judgement-bound enforcement 0.55, state-bound gate 0.66. With thinking, gates within noise (0.95 vs 0.88 at S=10).
quote: showing the record is the best rung
limits: Episode counts for tau2 and PM-Bench not stated in the part read; PM-Bench ledger value inferred. Corrupting compiled state degrades gate success monotonically.
agent_relevance: A gate is only as good as the check behind it. Gate only the tests, tool results and counters we can compute; leave judgement items as advice or as a second reader.

source: Zhang, Kweon, Han (2026) How Strongly Should Task State Influence an LLM Agent? (ticking without doing)
finding: Agents mark state in their own ledger and still repeat or skip steps. Of the on-turn re-executions, nearly all were steps the agent had already marked done. This is a measured LLM analogue of ticking an item without acting on it.
numbers: Self-ledger: a mark written in every episode (median 17 and 22 marks). Re-executions 27 (S=10) and 21 (S=15) per 128 episodes; 24 of 26 and 20 of 20 on-turn re-executions were of steps already marked done. Raw transcript errors per 128 episodes at S=10: 70 re-executions, 31 premature, 35 omissions. Enforcement gate used 0.92x (S=10) and 0.79x (S=15 dense) the tokens of raw transcript.
limits: Small model often wrote the booking line as a citation, which may overstate the failure. Qwen3-235B no-think only for these counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 gets LLM data: written marks are not proof of action. Ledger entries and checklist ticks need an outside read-back. Gating can also cost fewer tokens, not more.

source: Li et al. (2025; EMNLP 2026) SOPBench: Evaluating Language Agents at Following SOPs and Constraints
finding: Executable benchmark with 167 tools, 7 domains, 903 cases and rule-based verifiers. A case passes only if the final database state is right AND the required check functions were called before the action. Many models skip checks.
numbers: Overall pass rate (%), row alignment from PDF text approximate: o4-mini-high 76.08, Gemini-2.0-Flash-Thinking 67.66, DeepSeek-R1 62.13, GPT-4o 62.13, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 54.26, Gemini-2.0-Flash 33.33, Qwen2.5-7B 11.30. Only 5 models above 60%. Appended 'use the most appropriate tool asap' cut pass rates sharply (largest relative drop 60.1% in Figure 6; Claude-3.7-Sonnet singled out). Non-reasoning models fall as constraints rise (Gemini-2.0-Flash to about 20% above 5 constraints).
quote: can be easily jailbroken to overlook SOPs and constraints
limits: Customer-service tool domains; temperature 0; per-model table cells are scrambled in the PDF text so single values should be re-checked. Not a test of a gate.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: right outcome by skipped procedure is scored as a separate failure, and time pressure in the prompt makes skipping worse. Our harness should score 'was the check run' separately from 'was the answer right'.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in LLMs (factored vs joint, re-opened)
finding: Answering verification questions in a fresh prompt without the draft beats answering them in the same context. An explicit cross-check step adds more.
numbers: Llama 65B few-shot. Wikidata list precision: baseline 0.17, joint 0.29, factored 0.32, two-step 0.36. MultiSpanQA F1: 0.39 baseline, 0.46 joint, 0.48 factored. Longform FACTSCORE: 55.9 baseline, 60.8 joint, 63.7 factored, 71.4 factor+revise. Wiki-Category (Table 4, general questions): joint 0.15 vs factored 0.22.
quote: verifying questions should not attend to the original baseline response as they may be prone to repeating it
limits: No equal-token or equal-call comparison; factored uses many more prompts. No best-of-N control. Model checks itself, no tools. Llama 65B base, not a chat model. The 2.95 negative-entity figure belongs to Llama 2 70B Chat CoT; Llama 65B few-shot is 0.98.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly: fresh-context checking beats in-context checking by 1.5 to 4 points here, but the cost-matched and best-of-N-controlled test is still missing.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing (ablation, re-opened)
finding: Same model, same loop. Removing the tool feedback removes the gain. The tool, not the act of reviewing, carries the improvement.
numbers: text-davinci-003 QA F1: HotpotQA CoT 46.1, CRITIC w/o tool 46.1, CRITIC 50.5; AmbigNQ 58.6 / 58.3 / 64.9; TriviaQA 74.5 / 74.7 / 80.6. GSM8K program-of-thought 70.1: CRITIC 72.2, CRITIC w/o tool 68.3 (-1.8). Benefit grows with model size (TabMWP +4.7, +9.4, +16.0 for 7B, 13B, 70B).
limits: Older models (text-davinci-003, gpt-3.5, LLaMA-2). Tool calls add tokens, so not equal budget. Search and interpreter tools only. Table text was scrambled by pdftotext; cell mapping checked against the paper's own text.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: checks with an outside signal (interpreter, retrieval) give the gain; the same review step without it is flat or negative. Sort G-checks by whether a tool backs them.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction
finding: Survey of self-correction work. Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists. No prior work shows success with prompted self-feedback, except in tasks unusually suited to it. Fine-tuning at scale can teach it.
numbers: Survey, no single effect size (abstract page only).
limits: Abstract read, not the full survey. Review scope ends early 2024.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 backing: a second independent source, with Huang, that prompt-only review is not reliable. Treat pure self-review checks as suspect until measured on our tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies
finding: At matched budget (20 queries or 10k tokens per question) self-consistency matches or beats multi-agent debate and Reflexion. Debate and Reflexion plateau or get worse as budget grows.
numbers: 100 questions per dataset, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mainly. SC 20 samples; MAD 6 agents x 3 rounds (18 queries); Reflexion 10 proposals + 9 reflections (19). GPT-4 self-evaluation accuracy: GSM8K 0.937, MATH 0.707, TheoremQA 0.547, HotpotQA 0.675, CSQA 0.901. Reflexion with a GPT-4 evaluator still below Reflexion with SC.
limits: Only 100 questions per dataset; exact scores in figures only. Older models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 7: once call count is matched, much of the checker gain is just sampling more. Any factored or two-checker design must be compared to plain best-of-N at the same tokens.

source: Wunderlich et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Reasoning Improves Compute Efficiency: Pareto-Optimal Test-Time Scaling
finding: Counter-result: with compute matched on a Pareto front, debate and Mixture-of-Agents (different models as proposers) edge past self-consistency on MMLU-Pro. Self-refinement stays below plain CoT.
numbers: MMLU-Pro, n=1000, Llama 3.1 70B/8B. CoT 64.3%. Best SC 68.7% (10 samples), debate 70.0% (4 agents, 2 layers), MoA 71.4% (5 models, 4 layers). At comparable compute debate +1.3 and MoA +2.7 points over SC. SC saturates near 10 samples, debate near 4 agents; MoA keeps rising.
quote: Self-refinement consistently yields lower accuracy than the CoT baseline
limits: The 95% interval at n=1000 is about plus or minus 3 points, so +1.3 is within noise and +2.7 is borderline. One benchmark, one model family.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partial: mixing different models (different views) may beat repeating one. Not a clean test of a checker pair, and the effect is small.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs?
finding: Across seven benchmarks, majority voting alone accounts for most of the gain usually credited to multi-agent debate. Debate is proved to be a martingale on belief: no expected drift toward the truth.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B average accuracy: single agent 0.7205, decentralized MAD 0.7377 (T=2), 0.7112 (T=3), 0.7050 (T=5); centralized MAD T=2 0.6551. Voting about equals MAD in most cells. Also checked with Llama3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-32B.
quote: Majority Voting alone accounts for most of the performance gains typically attributed to MAD
limits: Small open models for the main table; the martingale proof is a model of debate, not of every protocol. Targeted updates toward correction can help.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 7: a second checker who sees the first one's answer adds little. If we add redundancy, keep checkers independent and aggregate, not converse.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: Over 350 LLMs: model errors are strongly correlated. On one leaderboard dataset, models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong. Shared architecture and shared provider raise the correlation; bigger, more accurate models are more correlated even across providers.
numbers: 350+ models, two leaderboards and a resume-screening task. 60% agreement when both models err (one dataset).
limits: Abstract page only; LLM-as-judge figures not read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: Hutchins-style redundancy needs independent failure modes. A second LLM checker of the same family shares the first one's blind spots, so use tools, retrieval or a different view to get real independence.

source: Sinha et al. (2025) The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs
finding: With plan and knowledge supplied, models still fail long tasks on execution. Per-step error rises as earlier errors stay in context (self-conditioning), and scale does not remove it; thinking does reduce it.
numbers: Key-value dictionary addition task, dictionary given in context. Best open model Qwen3-32B falls below 50% accuracy within 15 turns despite near-perfect first-step accuracy. Without thinking, DeepSeek-V3 fails at about four steps in one turn; R1 over 100; GPT-5 'Horizon' over 2100; Claude-4 Sonnet 432.
quote: Models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors from prior turns
limits: Synthetic retrieve-and-add task; it tests state carrying, not a written ledger of constants. No arm gives the model a verified ledger to read back.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 only indirect: long runs decay because the model carries running state in its own error-filled context. Supports writing state out and resetting context, but a ledger-vs-recompute test is still missing.

source: Tam et al. (2024) Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on LLM Performance
finding: Forcing structured output formats (JSON, XML, YAML) lowers reasoning accuracy for a fixed model, and stricter formats hurt more.
numbers: Abstract only: significant decline in reasoning under format restrictions; no figures read.
quote: we observe a significant decline in LLMs reasoning abilities under format restrictions
limits: Abstract page only; models and sizes not read. Later work may dispute the size of the effect (not opened here).
agent_relevance: Gap 6: an interface-only change (output format) moves reasoning accuracy for a fixed model outside code. Use free reasoning first, then a format step.

source: He et al. (2024) Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance?
finding: Same content in plain text, Markdown, JSON or YAML changes accuracy for the same model on reasoning, code generation and translation.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo varies by up to 40% on a code translation task by template; GPT-4 is less sensitive.
limits: Abstract page only; GPT models only. The largest swing is a code task, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: format sensitivity is real and shrinks with a stronger model. Fix one tested format for checklists and tool outputs and re-test it when the model changes.

source: Degani & Wiener (1991) Human Factors of Flight-Deck Checklists: The Normal Checklist (NASA CR-177549)
finding: The 71-page NASA report behind Degani & Wiener 1993. It reviews checklist function, formats and misuse. It gives no rates of skipped items: ASRS narratives were deliberately not analysed statistically because of reporting bias.
numbers: Takeoff, approach and landing are 27% of flight time but 76.3% of hull-loss accidents (Lautman & Gallimore 1988). Three checklist-related accidents in 15 months (Air New Orleans BAe J-31, Northwest 255 MD-80, Delta 1141 B-727). ASRS 1981-1989 and NTSB 1983-1988 searched; narratives used as illustration only.
quote: Indeed, it carries the risk that some pilots might choose not to use the checklist or conduct it poorly because of its length.
limits: 1991 report, not the 1993 Human Factors paper, which I could not open. No empirical skip rates exist in this source. Item selection is argued, not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly closed: no empirical skip rates in the primary NASA report. Cite it for design argument only, and for the item-selection tension (critical-only lists versus long legal lists).

source: Degani & Wiener (1991) NASA CR-177549 (challenge-response vs do-list, redundancy)
finding: Challenge-response keeps two redundancies: configuration redundancy (the list only checks what was already set from memory) and mutual redundancy (two crew verify). The do-list method drops configuration redundancy and a mistake passes unnoticed once the sequence is interrupted.
numbers: No numbers. Northwest 255: TAXI checklist normally done within 1-2 minutes of moving; interruptions meant the usual external cue vanished and the list was missed.
quote: due to the elimination of the configuration redundancy, a mistake can easily pass unnoticed once the sequence is interrupted
limits: Qualitative; the interruption account comes from the NTSB report as quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and design: our checks should verify work already done (a read-back), not lead the work as a cookbook, and should survive interruption by tying to a cue (a state change) rather than to order.

source: GitAuto engineering posts (2026) Our agent had the checklist and ignored it
finding: Practitioner report: a 41-check quality checklist in the system prompt was ignored for 3 categories; the fix was to report the specific failed checks back to the agent and gate completion on them. Seen only in a search snippet, not opened.
numbers: 41 checks, 3 never addressed (as summarised by search tool; not verified).
limits: Blog level, one team, no controls. Not opened. A companion claim of 70 to 90% prompt compliance versus near 100% for hooks (agentpatterns.ai) has no cited source.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 anecdote only; agrees in direction with Zhang 2026 but should not be cited as evidence.
